☆ An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
Yingli Wang, Lingjiong Zhu
Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.

Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.

A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.

All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.

We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $ρ_{\mathrm{eff}} = ρ(e^{ζq} - 1) / (ζq)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.

Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.

In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.

BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

Specifically, when $α>ν$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $Ω\bigl(η^{-(2+d/ν)}\min\{1,KT^{d/α}\}\bigr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $ν$ the smoothness, and $(K,α)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. ♻ ☆ Temporal Leakage in LLM Backtesting: Measurement, Validation, and Adjusted Scores
Zeyu Zhang, Bradly C. Stadie
The standard check for contamination in LLM backtests is simple: compare scores before and after the training cutoff. We show this check is uninformative. Four flagship models fail it on questions they cannot have memorized: every scored question resolved after their cutoffs. The reason is structural. Models legitimately know more about times near their cutoff, so recency mimics leakage, and we prove no passive backtest can separate the two from genuine skill. Measurement, not just detection, requires information from outside the backtest. We supply it in two forms. A known cutoff identifies leakage at the boundary; a matched clean control identifies it globally and yields a leakage-adjusted score. Under a convex-pull model, leakage concentrates on outcomes that surprised the crowd and that training covered well. Partial memorization gives a large part of the full inflation. In twin models with planted leakage, the estimators detect and localize it, track its dose, and return null on clean questions. On frontier models, the estimators detect one cutoff-localized signature. They find no significant leakage at the tested boundaries in five models with positive naive gaps. Backtests need not be discarded; they need one defensible reference.

♻ ☆ The Dynamic-Probabilistic Consistency Gap in Chaotic Surrogate Modeling NeurIPS 2026
Andre Herz, Matthijs Pals, Daniel Durstewitz, Georgia Koppe
Dynamical systems reconstruction (DSR) aims to learn surrogate models that capture the dynamics underlying time-series data. Reliable scientific inference with these surrogates requires uncertainty estimates consistent with the learned dynamics. We expose a dynamic-probabilistic consistency (DPC) gap: optimizing finite-horizon probabilistic objectives can degrade the learned dynamics or decouple predictive uncertainty from the local tangent dynamics it should reflect. We isolate three mechanisms behind this gap: core collapse, noise masking, and blind uncertainty. Specifically, we show that open-loop rollout objectives can penalize covariance growth driven by the dynamics, encouraging optimization shortcuts that weaken local expansion. To mitigate this gap, we propose KAFFEE (Kalman-Aware Framework For Ergodic Emulation), a differentiable extended Kalman filter-based training framework that jointly learns dynamics and noise covariances by coupling filtered innovation likelihoods with covariance propagation through learned local Jacobians, while differentiating through the Kalman updates. On stochastic hyperchaotic Lorenz-96, KAFFEE mitigates the identified failure modes and improves both reconstruction of dynamical invariants and predictive scores relative to open-loop objectives. The DPC gap also appears when probabilistically adapting a DSR foundation model across 13 chaotic systems, where KAFFEE improves predictive likelihood over open-loop adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's long-term dynamics and enabling in-context Bayesian filtering.

More importantly, this perspective exposes support selection as a central design axis rather than a byproduct of a particular parameterization. In practice, however, characterization still relies largely on factorial design of experiments (DOE) approaches, which are inefficient for resolving multivariate pass/fail boundaries in higher-dimensional spaces. While Bayesian optimization has transformed process optimization, adaptive methods for multi-objective process characterization remain lacking. Here, we introduce JAREX (Joint Acceptable Region EXploration), a Bayesian active-learning acquisition function for multi-objective process characterization. JAREX formulates characterization as a joint boundary-learning problem and adaptively selects experiments to recover the joint pass region defined by simultaneous satisfaction of threshold criteria across multiple objectives. JAREX combines an optimistic joint-feasibility mask with a multi-objective extension of randomized straddle, focusing sampling on the joint edge of failure. Our benchmark study suggests that JAREX provides more accurate and sample-efficient recovery of the joint pass region than factorial DOE, space-filling designs, and greedy objective-wise strategies over the full experimental budget range. For batched experimentation, it reduces the number of iterative process characterization experiments by more than half while preserving high accuracy for the boundary-identification task. Implemented in the open-source obsidian package, JAREX provides a modular framework for adaptive, data-efficient multi-objective algorithmic process characterization, supporting sample-efficient range finding in high-dimensional spaces.

Several methods in statistics and machine learning target a probability distribution for which an entropy-regularised variational objective is minimised. This increased flexibility introduces a computational challenge, as one loses access to an explicit unnormalised density for the target. To mitigate this difficulty, we introduce a novel measure of suboptimality called 'gradient discrepancy', and in particular a kernel gradient discrepancy (KGD) that can be explicitly computed. In the Bayesian statistics context, KGD coincides with the kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD), and we obtain a novel characterisation of KSD as measuring the size of a variational gradient. Outside this familiar setting, KGD enables novel sampling algorithms to be developed and compared, even when unnormalised densities cannot be obtained. To illustrate this point several novel algorithms are proposed and studied, including a natural generalisation of Stein variational gradient descent, with applications to mean-field neural networks and predictively oriented posteriors presented. On the theoretical side, our principal contribution is to establish sufficient conditions for desirable properties of KGD, such as continuity and convergence control.

Transformers integrate information from multiple past positions through sparse attention patterns that copy from specific locations. We study how these patterns form during training in a high-order Markov-chain setting, where the next token depends on several groups of past positions with differing statistical importance. Learning proceeds in discrete stages, each marked by the emergence of a sparse attention pattern for the next most important group. The dynamics are initially competitive, with all attention heads focusing on the dominant pattern, but later become cooperative, with different heads specializing in distinct patterns. For a tractable surrogate, the dynamics reduce to those of a tensor factorization problem, enabling us to prove stagewise convergence. Empirically, the number of stages completed depends on training set size, suggesting a form of implicit complexity control through early stopping. Overall, we give a theoretical account of how structured attention patterns and head specialization emerge without an explicit curriculum.

We show how this graph can be transformed to compute posterior covariances, and how equality saturation can be used to perform algebraic simplifications required for computation under specific prior choices. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free marginal coverage, yet standard split conformal uses a single global residual quantile and can adapt poorly to heteroscedasticity. We propose LoBoost, a model-native local conformal method that reuses the fitted ensemble's leaf structure to define a multiscale partition of the feature space. Each input is represented by the sequence of leaves it visits along the boosting path, and matching leaf prefixes define nested groups in which residual quantiles are estimated locally. By reusing the predictive structure already learned by the model, LoBoost requires no auxiliary partition or nuisance model, no retraining, and no additional data split beyond standard conformal calibration. Our theory connects the stability of the fitted ensemble and the geometry of its induced cells to local residual-score homogeneity, providing finite-sample coverage-error control and asymptotic pointwise validity as the local calibration size grows and the cells become sufficiently homogeneous. Experiments show a transparent quality-cost trade-off: LoBoost improves over global split conformal on several heterogeneous datasets, but it is not uniformly superior to the adaptive baselines and is not uniformly Pareto-optimal.
comment: Accepted paper version
♻ ☆ Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
Eric Price, Kevin Tian, Zhiyang Xun, Yusong Zhu
Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^3 m/\varepsilon^5)$-query estimator of Meel et al. (2025), where $m \geq K$ is the total size of the token alphabet. (2) Under logit access, we use $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, and this is tight. (3) Under noisy logit access, we smoothly interpolate between the above two guarantees: if probability values are given to relative error $σ$, we use $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2σ^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithms, for example measuring the distance between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights. Our experiments highlight the robustness and practicality of estimating the total variation distance, which remains estimable where the KL divergence is infinite. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation.
comment: Preliminary version of this paper is accepted by Neurips 2026. 40 pages, 11 figures, code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation
♻ ☆ Scalable and Calibrated Sampling for Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model via Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo
Youngsoo Baek, Andrea Agazzi, Felipe A. Medeiros, Samuel I. Berchuck
Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are widely used for analyzing correlated data, particularly in large-scale biomedical and social science applications. Scalable Bayesian inference for GLMMs is challenging due to an intractable marginal likelihood and a high computational cost incurred by conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. We develop a stochastic gradient MCMC (SGMCMC) algorithm tailored to GLMMs that enables accurate posterior inference in the large-sample regime. Our approach uses Fisher's identity to construct a (biased) Monte Carlo estimator of the gradient of the marginal log-likelihood, making SGMCMC feasible when direct gradient computation is impossible. We analyze the additional variability, introduced by both data subsampling and gradient approximation, to derive a post-hoc covariance correction that yields properly calibrated posterior uncertainty. We show through simulated studies that the proposed method provides accurate posterior means and variances in settings with a large number of groups, outperforming existing approaches, including control variate methods. We further demonstrate the method's practical utility in an analysis of electronic health records data, where accounting for variance inflation materially changes scientific conclusions.

♻ ☆ Gaussian mixture models in Hilbert spaces via kernel methods
Daniel López-Montero, Antonio Álvarez-López, Marcos Matabuena
Modern datasets across many disciplines increasingly consist of time-evolving, potentially infinite-dimensional random objects, such as dynamic functional data, which are naturally modeled in Hilbert spaces. In these settings, characterizing probability measures, for example, through densities, can be ill-defined or technically challenging. Motivated by clustering applications, we propose a Gaussian mixture framework for Hilbert-space-valued data based on kernel mean embeddings and develop efficient optimization algorithms for estimation. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed algorithm is well-defined and that the model yields a dense class of approximations in infinite-dimensional spaces. We evaluate the framework through extensive experiments on diverse data geometries, including $L^2$-functional data and graph signals arising in modern medical applications.

♻ ☆ Low-degree lower bounds via almost orthonormal bases
Alexandra Carpentier, Simone Maria Giancola, Christophe Giraud, Nicolas Verzelen
Low-degree polynomials have emerged as a powerful paradigm for providing evidence of statistical--computational gaps across a variety of high-dimensional statistical models [Wein25]. For detection problems---where the goal is to test a planted distribution $\mathbb{P}'$ against a null distribution $\mathbb{P}$ with independent components---the standard approach is to bound the advantage using an $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{P})$-orthonormal family of polynomials. However, this method breaks down for estimation tasks or more complex testing problems where $\mathbb{P}$ has some planted structures, so that no simple $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{P})$-orthogonal polynomial family is available. To address this challenge, several technical workarounds have been proposed [SW22,SW25], though their implementation can be delicate. In this work, we propose a more direct proof strategy. Focusing on random graph models, we construct a basis of polynomials that is almost orthonormal under $\mathbb{P}$, in precisely those regimes where statistical--computational gaps arise. This almost orthonormal basis not only yields a direct route to establishing low-degree lower bounds, but also allows us to explicitly identify the polynomials that optimize the low-degree criterion. This, in turn, provides insights into the design of optimal polynomial-time algorithms. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by recovering known low-degree lower bounds, and establishing new ones for problems such as hidden subcliques, stochastic block models, and seriation models.

♻ ☆ Density-Ratio Losses for Post-Hoc Learning to Defer NeurIPS 2026
Alexander Soen, Ragnar Thobaben, Joakim Jaldén, Richard Nock
We study post-hoc Learning to Defer (L2D) through the lens of ideal distributions: divergence-regularized reweightings of the data distribution under which a model attains low task loss. We define deferral via the density-ratio between a model's and an expert's ideals. Using the reduction from density-ratio estimation to class-probability estimation, we derive the DR CPE losses for post-hoc L2D scorers. Deferral decisions are then made by thresholding the scorer. For KL-based ideal distributions, our deferral rule recovers Chow's rule under the original distribution and a connection to an expert-tilted Bayes posterior---which incorporates the expert's performance---depending on if the ideal distributions are marginal or joint distributions. This leads to two variants of the DR CPE losses, with the joint variant being computationally convenient in practice. We establish consistency properties of the joint DR CPE losses when considering the zero-one task loss and strongly proper composite CPE losses. Experimentally, our approach is competitive compared to common baselines and is more robust across dataset settings. More broadly, our results cast post-hoc L2D as density-ratio estimation between ideal distributions, bridging Chow-style rules, expert comparison, and elucidating connections to related learning settings including anomaly detection.
comment: NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
Zikun Ye, Jiameng Lyu, Rui Tao
Artificial intelligence provides low-cost predictions for many analytics tasks, but their reliability and the value of another human label vary across tasks. We study how to allocate a shared human-validation budget when task-level uncertainty is unknown and each acquired label informs both estimation and subsequent allocation. For known difficulty levels, the benchmark follows a cost-adjusted Neyman rule that accounts for task importance and label cost. Within our Tuned Rectification-Difficulty framework, we develop an upper-confidence-bound policy that jointly learns the correction coefficients of tuned prediction-powered inference and the resulting difficulties from paired human labels and predictions, and establish an allocation-regret guarantee for the confidence-radius policy. In synthetic experiments and a real digital-twin survey with 68 tasks and over 2,000 respondents, our method closes most of the gap to the oracle on the allocation objective. It matches the estimation error of uniform allocation with up to 22.7% and 4.5% fewer human labels, respectively. The same allocation structure extends beyond scalar means to vector-valued decision models, including regression and choice/conjoint estimation, by replacing the scalar residual variance with a scalarized sandwich covariance. The value of AI depends not only on model accuracy but also on the operational policy that targets human oversight where it matters most.
♻ ☆ Where Has the Foreign Signal Gone? Contributor Composition and the Reliability of Social Media Sentiment
Piyush Akimitsu Ulrich Hounyo
Social media sentiment is increasingly used to predict stock returns. Its reliability depends on the composition of the crowd generating the feed. For foreign firms, the home-market investors who know them best are underrepresented on English-language Twitter. Hence, their feed should carry a less precise signal. Reduced-form analysis of firm-level Twitter sentiment shows that sentiment noise predicts next-quarter losses less consistently for foreign stocks than for domestic stocks. The loss-on-noise slope is negative in 78 percent of quarters for domestic stocks but in only 48 percent for foreign stocks, with a significant mean difference in slopes. We interpret this difference through a noisy rational expectations model in which the feed carries a public signal produced by three types of contributors. Specialists post repeatedly with information about the firm, attention-driven contributors post once with information about the firm and a transient fad, and automated accounts post repeatedly with no information about the firm. The share of each contributor type and the size of the fad determine the precision of the signal, which, in turn, determines how much of the feed's noise reaches prices. The model gives repeat-author share, fad and precision from the vendor's aggregate metrics, without account-level data, whereas prior work backs out precision from price informativeness. The structural estimates show that feeds for foreign stocks have a higher share of repeat authors, a larger fad component and a less precise signal. Thus, the foreign signal did not disappear but got diluted.
♻ ☆ Do we really need the Rademacher complexities?
Daniel Bartl, Shahar Mendelson
We study the fundamental problem of learning with respect to the squared loss in a convex class. In the subgaussian setting, the sharpest known sample complexity bounds are characterised via fixed points associated with the limiting gaussian process. In more general settings (for example, heavier-tailed scenarios) the state-of-the-art bounds rely on localised Rademacher complexities, which are often difficult to control and can be considerably larger than their limiting gaussian counterparts. We show that if one has access to coarse information on the covariance structure of the underlying class, it is possible to derive an upper bound on the sample complexity that matches the state-of-the-art rates in the gaussian setting---even in heavy-tailed regimes. As a consequence, under rather minimal assumptions, learning problems that share the same $L_2$-structure---even those involving heavy-tailed distributions---admit the same upper bound on the sample complexity as if the problem were fully gaussian. This constitutes the first universality result for general convex learning problems. The proof is based on a novel learning procedure, and its performance is studied by combining optimal mean estimation techniques for real-valued random variables with Talagrand's generic chaining method.
♻ ☆ Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles NeurIPS
Binh Duc Vu, David S. Watson
Tree ensembles such as random forests (RFs) and gradient boosting machines (GBMs) are among the most widely used supervised learners, yet their theoretical properties remain incompletely understood. We adopt a spectral perspective on these algorithms, with two main contributions. First, we derive minimax-optimal convergence for RF regression, showing that, under mild regularity conditions on tree growth, the eigenvalue decay of the induced kernel operator governs the statistical rate. Second, we exploit this spectral viewpoint to develop compression schemes for tree ensembles. For RFs, leading eigenfunctions of the kernel operator capture the dominant predictive directions; for GBMs, leading singular vectors of the smoother matrix play an analogous role. Learning nonlinear maps for these spectral representations yields distilled models that are orders of magnitude smaller than the originals while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our methods compare favorably to state of the art algorithms for forest pruning and rule extraction, with applications to resource constrained computing.
comment: NeurIPS camera ready version. 10 pages main text, 48 pages total (excluding checklist), with 12 figures and 10 tables total
♻ ☆ Eigenvalues of the Hessian in Deep Learning: The Origin of Symmetry and Its Breaking
Yossi Arjevani
Hessian spectra at trained models in deep learning exhibit a persistent pattern: eigenvalues organize into distinct clusters, including a large bulk near zero and a few isolated outliers. This paper shows that a natural account of these spectral phenomena emerges when the original setting is understood as a departure from a nearby, otherwise hidden, highly symmetric reference. Modifications, including changes to the architecture, data distribution, or parameter metric, expose a nearby reference configuration whose Hessian exhibits rich invariances-ones not accounted for by weight symmetries. There, symmetry enables a precise description of the spectra, forcing high-dimensional kernels and eigenvalues of large multiplicity. Returning to the original configuration breaks the Hessian symmetry and thereby produces the observed hierarchy of clusters and outliers. The framework is developed in some generality, with a detailed analysis of three-layer ReLU networks and applications to convolutional, graph, and transformer models, as well as to the NTK. The same mechanism is further shown to yield analogous spectral structures in layerwise Hessians and the Gauss-Newton matrix.
♻ ☆ Factor Augmented High-Dimensional SGD
Shubo Li, Yuefeng Han, Xiufan Yu
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a fundamental optimization algorithm widely used in modern machine learning. In this paper, we propose Factor-Augmented SGD (FSGD), a new optimization method that leverages latent factor representations in high-dimensional learning tasks. Unlike standard two-stage dimension reduction approaches that rely on offline representation learning and full data storage, a key novelty of FSGD is that it operates purely on streaming data, making it scalable to large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Furthermore, we establish the first theoretical framework that explicitly incorporates latent factor estimation error into the analysis of SGD, and provide moment convergence in $\ell^s$ norm under decaying step sizes and mini-batch updates. Our results provide a new foundation for employing SGD reliably and scalably in high-dimensional machine learning systems.
♻ ☆ A Distribution Mapping Approach to Counterfactually Fair Reinforcement Learning NeurIPS 2026
Jianhan Zhang, Jitao Wang, John D. Piette, Donglin Zeng, Chengchun Shi, Zhenke Wu
Reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to optimize sequential decisions to maximize population-level benefits over time. However, when deployed in high-stakes settings such as healthcare, RL decisions might systematically restrict some subpopulation's access to valuable services in a manner contrary to the values and goals of stakeholders. Counterfactual fairness (CF) offers a promising framework to address this problem based on causal reasoning. This paper develops a data preprocessing algorithm that, when used in tandem with policy learning, enables CF in RL. Our algorithm relies on a novel quantile distribution mapping method for sequentially estimating the counterfactual states and rewards in the data preprocessing step, subsuming common additivity assumptions used for counterfactual prediction as a special case. We theoretically prove that the per-step level of counterfactual unfairness and infinite-horizon suboptimality gap can be bounded under mild regularity conditions. We also empirically test our algorithm in numerical experiments as well as in application to a real-world interventional digital health dataset.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Posterior Contraction Rates for Sparse Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Anisotropic Besov Spaces
Jeunghun Oh, Jaeyong Lee, Lizhen Lin, Kyeongwon Lee
We study posterior contraction rates for sparse Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) over anisotropic Besov spaces, providing a statistical foundation for KANs from a Bayesian point of view. We show that sparse Bayesian KANs equipped with spike-and-slab-type sparsity priors attain a near-minimax posterior contraction rate. In particular, the contraction rate depends on the intrinsic anisotropic smoothness of the underlying function. Moreover, by placing a hyperprior on a single model-size parameter, the resulting posterior adapts to unknown anisotropic smoothness and still achieves the corresponding near-minimax rate. A distinctive feature of our results, compared with those for standard multilayer perceptrons, is that the KAN depth can be kept fixed: owing to the expressive power of learnable spline edge functions, the required approximation complexity is controlled through the network width, the range and size of the spline grid, and parameter sparsity. Our analysis develops theoretical tools tailored to sparse spline-edge architectures, including approximation and complexity bounds for Bayesian KANs. We then extend to compositional Besov spaces and show that the contraction rates depend on layerwise smoothness and effective dimension of the underlying compositional structure, thereby effectively avoiding the curse of dimensionality. Together, these results advance the theoretical understanding of Bayesian neural networks and establish rigorous Bayesian guarantees for KANs.
♻ ☆ The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning NeurIPS 2024
Oscar Leong, Eliza O'Reilly, Yong Sheng Soh
Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.

☆ ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking
Xiang Fang, Wanlong Fang, Junhao Dong, Daizong Liu
Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Multimedia
☆ Multimodal Judges Flag, Humans Decide: A Review-and-Edit Framework for AI-Generated Product Video Ads WACV 2027
Anoubhav Agarwaal, Sukesh Perla, Karthikeyan Mohanraj, Susmita Ghose
Generative pipelines can now turn every product page of an e-commerce catalog into a short video ad, but deciding whether such an ad is usable is not one good-or-bad call. We describe how we operationalized the review and editing of these ads so that both can keep pace with generation: reviewers go through each ad scene by scene and answer six questions, on the product, scene quality, pronunciation, script, sound and captions; judges built from vision-language, speech and language models file each finding under the matching question, and reviewers accept or reject each finding and add what the judges missed. Each confirmed issue then opens an edit tool matched to it. The questions and the routing from a finding to its fix do not depend on the models that generate the ad. Across 120 ads from our pipeline, reviewed with judge findings on screen, reviewers marked the product wrong on 60% of scenes, and script, caption or sound problems on under 10% each. On 60 of these ads, they marked the product wrong on 58% of scenes, far more than the 26% marked by two reviewers who later saw the ads with the judges hidden; one reviewer who saw the ads both ways marked 57% with judge findings and 19% without. On 120 blind-labeled scenes, a product judge that watches the clip with the catalog photos reached AUC 0.84, while video-quality and photo-similarity scores were close to chance. We tune the judges for recall: the product judge catches nearly all defects but also flags many clean scenes, so reviewers decide; together, the judges widen what reviewers mark and reviewers add what the judges miss. Without judge findings, one reviewer's marking faded over a session. We release a review-portal template and our review data (120 ads and 562 scenes with judge findings and human marks, plus 120 blind-labeled scenes with baseline scores) at https://github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit.

☆ Artifact Filtering versus Artifact-Compensated Training in JPEG to JPEG AI Recompression
Igor Podtsepko, Yuriy Kim, Karam Mahfod, Evgeny Belyaev, Kristian Kirs, Jianping Lin, Ilya Papiev
In this paper, we consider the problem of recompression of images from JPEG to JPEG AI format. We show that direct recompression from JPEG to JPEG~AI trained on uncompressed images is accompanied by the preservation of the JPEG image artifacts in the resulting JPEG~AI image. In order to avoid it, we evaluate an approach where an artifacts removal neural network is first applied to the input JPEG image as an external pre-filter. However, in this case, the processing time is increased by 29 times. Therefore, we propose an artifact-compensated training for JPEG AI and show that it is able to combine pre-filtering against target distortions with efficient compression without increase in the processing time.

☆ BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
Taemin Cho, Hector Martel, Enyan Koh
We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.
comment: Published in ISMIR 2026 (Best Paper Award nominee). Demo: https://bars-ismir2026.github.io/bars/
♻ ☆ Textual Response-Aware Guidance for Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features constrains all directions equally, providing broad coverage without semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. We therefore propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
♻ ☆ Memory-Efficient Active Perception for Embodied Question Answering in Dynamic Human-Populated Scenes
Xin Lu, Rui Li, Xun Huang, Weixin Li, Jiayuan Li, Chuanqing Zhuang, Zhengda Lu, Jun Xiao
Embodied Question Answering (EQA) couples active visual perception, vision-language reasoning, and sequential decision making, and has traditionally been evaluated in temporally stable environments where visual evidence can be accumulated reliably. In realistic multimedia settings such as dynamic human-populated scenes, however, moving people and transient occlusions introduce human-induced perceptual variations: task-relevant multimodal cues become transient, viewpoint-dependent, and incompletely captured in individual views. Conventional store-then-retrieve strategies generate redundant visual evidence and incur high inference cost, making them ill-suited to such variations. This exposes two core problems for embodied agents: resolving viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, and maintaining compact evidence for efficient inference. To address these challenges, we present DIVRR (Dynamic-Informed View Refinement with Relevance-guided Rotation and adaptive memory selection), a training-free active evidence-acquisition framework for EQA. DIVRR combines question-conditioned room guidance with relevance-triggered view augmentation to guide exploration and additional observation. Selective memory admission uses the same relevance signal as view augmentation to retain high-scoring evidence, reducing stored entries while keeping the retrieved visual context compact. To evaluate EQA under human-induced perceptual variations, we introduce DynHuman-EQA, a dynamic human-populated EQA dataset constructed in Habitat, comprising dynamic and static subsets under shared scene layouts. Experiments on DynHuman-EQA and HM-EQA show that DIVRR outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and memory efficiency. The gains are most pronounced in dynamic human-populated scenes.

☆ VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
Gokul Bhusal, Delanna Do, Ekaterina Merkurjev, Kevin Miller, Stephan Wojtowytsch
We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

☆ Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
Olga Isupova, Danil Kuzin, Fredrik Gustafsson, Lyudmila Mihaylova
This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.
☆ Continuous Horizon Forecasting
Malcolm Wolff, Elliott Zackrone, Souhaib Ben Taieb, Michael W. Mahoney, Kin G. Olivares
Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.

☆ Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
Kyle Parrella, Kejin Wu
GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

☆ Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
Shai Ben-David, Steve Hanneke, Farnam Mansouri, Amirreza Shaeiri
We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Granger causality has become one of the most widely used tools to infer directed interactions between the components of a system. The name however can be misleading: it detects predictive relations among the measured signals, not causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them. This article starts by reviewing recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis. It then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models, and asks under which conditions that structure can be read causally.

The results do not indicate that clique constraints uniformly accelerate optimisation. However, their benefit depends on graph density, sample size, and cut-management policy, while large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput. Tighter valid Big-M bounds reduced the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings, without necessarily changing SHD or F1 at a fixed time limit. These findings characterize the computational trade-offs of clique-constrained exact causal learning, and identify selective separation and incumbent repair as promising directions.

Generative modeling of discrete data, such as graphs, underpins many scientific and industrial applications, including molecular discovery and materials design. In these domains, probabilistic inference is particularly valuable, as it enables composable generation and principled incorporation of desired constraints, such as structural or functional properties. On molecular graph benchmarks, GEM matches or surpasses strong discrete diffusion baselines on most reported metrics. Beyond improving generation quality, GEM's relative likelihood modeling enables targeted exploration, facilitating compositional generation, property-constrained sampling, and interpolation between graphs. Project page: https://michalbalcerak.ai/graph-energy-matching/.

♻ ☆ Variance Reduction for Gradients from Diffusion Teachers NeurIPS 2026

The teacher gradients these pipelines consume are expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise, estimated by Monte Carlo (MC). Each MC draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding), so estimator variance dominates compute cost. We introduce CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework that casts these gradients as a classical two-stage sampling problem with asymmetric per-level costs. This motivates a hierarchical MC estimator that amortizes each expensive upstream computation by reusing it across cheap diffusion draws, with within-unit variance further reduced by timestep importance sampling (IS) and stratified inverse-CDF sampling. CARV delivers 2 to 3x effective compute multipliers on text-to-3D and data attribution without changing the objective. In text-to-3D, reuse provides most of the gain and IS with stratification adds about 25%. In single-step distillation, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude but do not improve downstream FID, marking the regime where MC variance is no longer the bottleneck.

One of its important applications consists of estimating a feedback gain matrix that can stabilize an unknown system. This paper focuses on the analysis of such adaptive stabilization schemes for multivariate linear time-invariant state-space models. The system instability practically renders trajectories short, i.e., the observed data is notably limited. So, it is crucial to tightly consider effects of \emph{all} involved quantities including length and number of trajectories, dimension, controllability Gramian, and signal-to-noise ratio. More specifically, this study shows that the strength of the excitation signal helps stabilization only \emph{logarithmically}; a very important phenomenon that we explain under the term \emph{signal saturation}.

For many technologies (\textit{e.g.} peer-to-peer networks, IoT, multi-agent systems), extending the ability to calculate consensus rankings with guarantees of convergence and resilience to potential contamination in a decentralized setting, when preference data is initially distributed across a communicating network, remains a major methodological challenge. Indeed, in recent years, the literature on decentralized computation has mainly focused on computing or optimizing statistics such as arithmetic means using gossip algorithms. The purpose of this article is precisely to study how to achieve reliable and resilient consensus on collective rankings in a decentralized setting, thereby raising new questions, robustness to corrupted nodes, and scalability through reduced communication costs in particular. The approach proposed and analyzed here relies on the robustness guarantees offered by random gossip communication, which allows autonomous agents to compute a global ranking consensus using local interactions only, without coordination or a central authority.

Luca Martino
In the last decades, energy-based models (EBMs) have become an important class of probabilistic models in which a component of the likelihood is intractable and therefore cannot be evaluated explicitly. Consequently, parameter estimation in EBMs is challenging for conventional inference methods. This work is a review paper that brings together these different methodological contributions within a unified framework, highlighting the connections among noise contrastive estimation (NCE), reverse logistic regression (RLR), Bennett's acceptance-ratio (BAR) method, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and bridge sampling within the context of EBMs. Some of them are equivalent under specific conditions. This unified perspective clarifies relationships among existing methods and enables the development of new estimators, with the potential to improve statistical and computational efficiency. Furthermore, this study helps elucidate the success of NCE in terms of its flexibility and robustness, while also identifying scenarios in which its performance can be further improved. Our aim is to provide a self-contained and accessible treatment, with clear and straightforward derivations, that brings together these contributions within a common framework and makes the main results and their underlying ideas understandable to a broader readership. The contribution is twofold. First, this work serves as a comprehensive tutorial for researchers entering the field, introducing the fundamental concepts and derivations. Second, it offers a thorough review for experienced practitioners. The code used in the numerical experiments is available to support the reproducibility of the results.

Unbalanced optimal transport extends classical optimal transport to measures with different total masses, but statistical guarantees for estimation of the transport map and the growth map remain limited. We study unbalanced optimal transport with quadratic cost and Kullback-Leibler marginal penalties and argue that the natural target of estimation is a transport-growth pair. Consequently, we develop two estimators for the transport-growth pair under two setups: a nearest-neighbor estimator for transporting between general densities, and a kernel-based estimator for transporting between smooth densities. We prove that the kernel-based estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor by deriving a matching lower bound on the minimax risk. Our main technical contribution is a reduction of estimation to a stability bound on the unbalanced optimal transport value. This bound controls the transport map and growth map risks through the duality gap of the true dual potentials for the estimated measures. These results provide a statistical foundation for estimation of the transport-growth pair in unbalanced optimal transport.

Separating externally forced trends from internal climate variability is a fundamental challenge in climate science, particularly when analyzing observational records that exist only as a single realization. We show that a single climate realization can be decomposed into forced and internal components by treating external forcing as a dynamical driver within a linear stochastic system, an idea grounded in pullback attractor theory. This addresses a central challenge for climate projection and for detecting and attributing the forced response. Existing single-realization methods rely on linear inverse models (LIMs), which ignore forcing, or linear regression, which omits dynamics. Here we introduce PullbackDMDc, a method grounded in non-autonomous dynamical systems theory and dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc), incorporating pullback attractor estimation to decompose a single climate realization into spatial modes and their associated forced and internal components, yielding a physically interpretable picture of the underlying dynamics. After testing on a synthetic system with a known forced response, we illustrate the utility of PullbackDMDc for Earth System Model (ESM) evaluation by applying it to near-surface air temperature and sea-level pressure from reanalysis and four ESM large ensembles. PullbackDMDc estimates the forced response with skill matching or exceeding established baselines and helps select forcing predictors against model-based ground truth. Its internal-variability components reveal that ESMs qualitatively capture interannual and decadal modes while exhibiting systematic differences relative to each other and to observations. Skillful forced-response estimation and a novel decomposition position PullbackDMDc as a practical tool for single-realization climate analysis and ESM evaluation.

Online learning with delayed feedback typically assumes that the learner can track all pending rounds until their feedback arrives. Combining these bounds with our schedulers yields regret guarantees for capacity-constrained OCO under convex and strongly convex losses, for both first-order and bandit feedback. For bandit feedback, the standard delayed BCO rates are instead modulated by $(1 + σ_{\text{max}}/C)$ factors, where $σ_{\text{max}}$ is the maximum number of outstanding observations. This allows the regret bound to degrade gracefully when $C < σ_{\text{max}}$. We complement our analysis with numerical experiments.

Yiming Sun, Mi Zhang
Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.

☆ TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption NeurIPS2026
Qiming Huang, Peixi Liu, Jianbo Jiao
Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.

The frequency path made no detectable difference: discriminative alone (standalone validation AUC 0.91-0.98 late in training) but of no marginal value under this fusion, at two feature widths of one 4.0 M trunk, every seed-pooled interval for the intra-dataset compression contrasts including zero; on the single held-out manipulation tested, the fair variants sat below the plain backbone. The evidence is FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era and single-codec. Match controls on training recipe as well as capacity, and buy compression robustness with codec diversity before architecture.

Our results recast adaptive Ref-AVS reasoning as a pre-decisional representation problem: before the first generated token, the generation-onset state contains linearly decodable information predictive of whether additional reasoning will improve segmentation. A linear probe predicts binary reasoning need with 70.1% accuracy, substantially outperforming text-only features and uncertainty-based proxy signals. As a router, the onset-state controller improves over downstream confidence routing and closely matches Short-then-Decide while using far fewer tokens. Proxy comparisons show that the onset representation contains predictive information not fully recovered by the evaluated hand-crafted features. Reusing this onset state for lightweight, single forward-pass routing reduces autoregressive token consumption by 60% while retaining about 96% of always-long performance. It further provides a cost-quality trade-off on $R^2$-AVSBench without target-label tuning, rather than an accuracy improvement over always-long. Error analysis links harmful long reasoning to phrase and localization drift, illustrating the benefit of bypassing unnecessary reasoning on simple queries. Ultimately, our results support efficient adaptive reasoning in Ref-AVS through pre-decisional internal representations.
